Diagnosis:
The current bug report states that the class ExtendedMessageFormat in the package org.apache.commons.lang3.text extends the java.text.MessageFormat class (or a similar superclass) but does not override the equals(Object) method. This omission is problematic because ExtendedMessageFormat adds additional fields (such as a registry of FormatFactory objects), so the default equals implementation inherited from the superclass will ignore these fields and potentially declare two ExtendedMessageFormat objects equal even if their registries differ.

This diagnosis is consistent with the supplied failing test case testEqualsHashcode(). The test creates ExtendedMessageFormat instances with different registries and patterns and checks for equality and hash code consistency. The test expects two instances with different registries (defined by different FormatFactories) to be considered not equal and also to have different hash codes. However, since ExtendedMessageFormat does not override equals, equality checks fall back on the superclass implementation, which does not consider the registry field. This leads to incorrect equality results and failing tests.

The constructor snippet shows ExtendedMessageFormat stores the registry field but does not evidence any equals or hashCode overrides considering this new field. Attempts to retrieve an equals method specific to ExtendedMessageFormat failed, confirming it does not exist. This matches the FindBugs warning about missing equals override when adding stateful fields.

Recent bug reports talk about missing equals(Object) overrides in classes defining covariant equals methods, a related but separate style problem that further highlights the standard practice of overriding equals when adding new fields.

In conclusion, the root cause of the bug is that ExtendedMessageFormat adds a new state field (registry) but does not override equals(Object) and hashCode() methods to properly consider this field in equality checks and hashing. The failing test cases fail because equality checks do not behave as expected when two instances differ in registry content.

The remedy would be to implement equals(Object) and hashCode() in ExtendedMessageFormat to incorporate the registry field and ensure correct behavior. The absence of these overrides leads to the fault observed.

Next, I would suggest reviewing or creating the equals and hashCode methods in ExtendedMessageFormat.
